did_you_know.text: Did you know? Hezekiah responded to the Assyrian threat by tearing his clothes, putting on sackcloth, and going to the house of the LORD—expressions of mourning, distress, and submission before God.
Did you know? Hezekiah’s messengers described Jerusalem’s condition as that of a woman in labor who lacked the strength to give birth, expressing the severity of the crisis.
Did you know? Isaiah prophesied that a spirit would be sent against Sennacherib, that he would hear a report, return to his own land, and there be killed by the sword.
Did you know? After receiving Sennacherib’s letters, Hezekiah went up to the house of the LORD and spread them out before the LORD—a gesture that turned a political threat into a prayer.
Did you know? In his prayer, Hezekiah asked for deliverance not only for Judah, but also so that all the kingdoms of the earth would know that the LORD alone is God.
Did you know? The LORD’s reply portrays Jerusalem as “Daughter Zion” and “Daughter Jerusalem,” mocking Sennacherib’s arrogance.
Did you know? The LORD uses the image of a hook in the nose and a bit in the lips to describe how he would stop Sennacherib and send him back by the way he had come.

Did you know? The sign given to Judah involved a gradual agricultural process: in the first year they would eat what grew on its own, in the second year what sprang from that, and in the third year they would sow, reap, plant vineyards, and eat their fruit.

Did you know? The promise to protect Jerusalem is stated in detail by negation: the Assyrian army would not enter the city, shoot an arrow there, advance against it with a shield, or build a siege ramp against it.
Did you know? According to the text, the angel of the LORD struck 185,000 people in the Assyrian camp; when the survivors arose in the morning, they found all the bodies dead.
